result: Loss of DLK and/or LZK does not affect postnatal development of Purkinje cells. The authors generated LZK knockout mice using CRISPR and combined these with conditional DLK knockout mice. Histological analysis, Purkinje cell counts, molecular layer thickness, astrocyte markers, and body weight were all normal in single and double knockout mice at P60.
evaluation: Claims C5, C46-C60 provide converging evidence from multiple knockout models showing no developmental defects in Purkinje cells. The data include appropriate controls, multiple quantitative measures (cell counts, layer thickness, body weight), and immunohistochemical validation. The conclusion is well-supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 1 and supplements.

result: Activating DLK in Purkinje cells causes rapid degeneration with early lethality. The authors generated Cre-inducible DLK overexpression mice and crossed them with PvalbCre mice. These mice showed reduced body weight, abnormal movements, cerebellar abnormalities, nearly complete Purkinje cell loss (~98%) by P21, reduced molecular layer thickness, and increased astrocyte/microglia reactivity.
evaluation: Claims C6, C62-C78 demonstrate rapid Purkinje cell degeneration following DLK activation. The evidence includes behavioral observations, quantitative histology, time-course analysis, and markers of neuroinflammation. The transgenic design is appropriate and the phenotype is severe and well-documented across multiple measures in Figure 2 and supplements.

result: DLK-induced Purkinje cell degeneration involves JNK pathway activation and apoptosis. Elevated DLK expression substantially increased p-c-Jun in Purkinje cells at P6. TUNEL assays showed increased apoptotic cells from P5-P15, with some co-localizing with Purkinje cells. A significant portion of Purkinje cells at P15 were positive for cleaved caspase-3.
evaluation: Claims C79-C87 establish the mechanistic basis of DLK-induced degeneration through JNK activation and apoptosis. The data include appropriate markers (p-c-Jun, TUNEL, cleaved caspase-3), time-course analysis, and co-localization studies shown in Figure 3 and supplements. The conclusion that DLK activates JNK and causes apoptotic cell death is well-supported.

result: DLK activation disrupts the dendritic cytoskeleton in Purkinje cells. DLK was detected in somas, dendrites, and axons. A substantial portion of Purkinje cells showed dendritic varicosities, with ~65% of swollen dendrites positive for cleaved caspase-3. MAP2 and NF-200 levels were significantly decreased in dendrites and axons.
evaluation: Claims C88-C100 demonstrate cytoskeletal disruption as a feature of DLK-induced degeneration. The data include immunolocalization, quantification of morphological abnormalities, and measurement of cytoskeletal protein levels shown in Figure 3. The association between dendrite swelling and apoptosis markers is quantified. However, the authors appropriately note uncertainty about whether cytoskeletal disruption is a direct effect or downstream consequence.

result: Activating LZK in Purkinje cells causes slow degeneration. PvalbCre/+;Hipp11-LZK(iOE)/+ mice survived to at least 8 months but had low body weight. Morphological abnormalities appeared around P15, with progressive cell loss from P21 to P120. The cerebellum area and molecular layer were significantly reduced. LZK expression and degeneration were more severe in anterior cerebellum, correlating with higher transgene expression.
evaluation: Claims C7, C101-C111 establish that LZK activation causes slow, progressive Purkinje cell degeneration, contrasting with rapid DLK-induced degeneration. The data include long-term survival analysis, quantitative histology over multiple time points, and spatial correlation between expression levels and degeneration severity shown in Figure 4 and supplements. The regional variation provides internal validation of the dose-response relationship.

result: LZK activation triggers JNK activation and caspase-mediated apoptosis with slow kinetics. Elevating LZK expression increased p-c-Jun in Purkinje cells at P90. Cleaved caspase-3 co-localized with Purkinje cells in LZK overexpression mice but not controls. The authors conclude that LZK triggers JNK and apoptosis but with slow degeneration kinetics, suggesting differential signaling regulation compared to DLK.
evaluation: Claims C112-C116 demonstrate that LZK activates similar pathways as DLK (JNK and apoptosis) but with different kinetics. The data include appropriate markers at relevant time points shown in Figure 4. The conclusion of differential signaling regulation is supported by the contrasting time courses of degeneration between DLK and LZK, though the molecular basis for this difference is not fully elucidated.

result: CELF2 deletion does not modify DLK-induced Purkinje cell degeneration. PvalbCre/+;Celf2fl/fl mice were normal. In PvalbCre/+;Celf2fl/fl;Hipp11-DLK(iOE)/+ mice, Purkinje cell degeneration was similar to PvalbCre/+;Hipp11-DLK(iOE)/+ mice. CELF2 deletion did not alter DLK expression levels or p-c-Jun induction. All pups died around P21 with similar morbidity.
evaluation: Claims C9, C123-C130 demonstrate that CELF2 deletion does not rescue DLK-induced degeneration. The data include appropriate controls, quantitative histology, protein expression analysis, and survival data shown in Figure 5 supplements. This negative result is important for establishing pathway specificity and is well-documented.

result: CELF2 deletion dramatically attenuates LZK-induced Purkinje cell degeneration. PvalbCre/+;Celf2fl/fl;Hipp11-LZK(iOE)/+ mice showed significantly improved behavioral phenotypes from P30-P120, though body weight remained low. CELF2 deletion dramatically reduced Purkinje cell degeneration with significant improvement in dendrite morphology at P120, inhibited astrogliosis and microgliosis, rescued MAP2 and NF-200 reduction, and suppressed pinceau disorganization.
evaluation: Claims C131-C139 demonstrate robust rescue of LZK-induced degeneration by CELF2 deletion. The data include behavioral assessments, quantitative histology, multiple cellular markers, and cytoskeletal protein analysis shown in Figure 5 and supplements. The rescue is dramatic and well-documented across multiple measures, providing strong evidence for CELF2's role in LZK signaling. The persistence of low body weight suggests some effects are not rescued, which is appropriately noted.

result: CELF2 regulates alternative splicing of Map2k7 (MKK7). Prior studies in T-cells showed that MKK7 activity is regulated through alternative splicing of exon 2, with CELF2 promoting exon skipping to produce a short, high-activity isoform. In cerebellum, CELF2 deletion reduced the mRNA ratio of Map2k7-S to Map2k7-L by ~20%.
evaluation: Claims C10, C119-C122, C140 establish CELF2's role in regulating MKK7 splicing. The mechanism is supported by prior literature (C119-C122) and validated in the current system by qRT-PCR showing a ~20% reduction in the short/long isoform ratio upon CELF2 deletion (C140, Figure 5 supplement 1B). The modest change in splicing ratio is consistent with partial rescue and suggests other factors may also contribute.

result: CELF2 deletion attenuates LZK-induced JNK signaling and apoptosis, supporting MKK7 as a functional mediator of LZK signaling. LZK expression levels were not altered by CELF2 deletion. However, CELF2 deletion significantly attenuated p-c-Jun intensity in Purkinje cells, significantly reduced TUNEL+ cells, and nearly eliminated cleaved caspase-3 signals in Purkinje cells. Increased pro-apoptotic Bcl-xL cleavage products in LZK overexpression mice were also observed.
evaluation: Claims C141-C150 establish the mechanistic link between CELF2, MKK7 splicing, and LZK signaling. The data show that CELF2 deletion reduces JNK activation (p-c-Jun) and apoptosis markers (TUNEL, cleaved caspase-3) without affecting LZK expression, shown in Figure 6 and supplements. The more prominent reduction in cleaved caspase-3 compared to p-c-Jun (noted in C176) suggests pathway complexity, which the authors appropriately acknowledge. The conclusion that MKK7 is a functional mediator of LZK signaling is well-supported.

result: DLK and LZK induce Purkinje cell degeneration independently of each other. In PvalbCre/+;Map3k13KO/KO;Hipp11-DLK(iOE)/+ mice, Purkinje cell degeneration and astrogliosis were similar to PvalbCre/+;Hipp11-DLK(iOE)/+ mice, with similar lethality at P21. LZK deletion did not affect DLK-induced p-c-Jun levels. Conversely, in PvalbCre/+;Map3k12fl/fl;Hipp11-LZK(iOE)/+ mice, Purkinje cell degeneration and astrogliosis were similar to PvalbCre/+;Hipp11-LZK(iOE)/+ mice. DLK deletion did not affect LZK-induced p-c-Jun levels.
evaluation: Claims C8, C154-C162 demonstrate that each kinase induces degeneration independently. The genetic epistasis experiments are well-designed, with deletion of one kinase failing to rescue degeneration induced by overexpression of the other. The data include quantitative histology, JNK activation markers, and survival analysis shown in Figure 7 and supplements. This establishes that DLK and LZK act through parallel rather than sequential or synergistic pathways in this context.

result: DLK and LZK are conserved MAP3Ks with similar biochemical properties. Both kinases can activate JNK via MKK4 or MKK7, share similar biochemical activities, undergo auto-activation via leucine-zipper-mediated dimerization dependent on protein abundance, and have nearly identical kinase domains. Therefore, elevating expression serves as a proxy for activation.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C15-C16, C40-C42, C117, C151 establish the background knowledge about DLK and LZK. These claims are supported by extensive prior literature (citations provided) and are consistent with established knowledge in the field. The inference that elevated expression serves as a proxy for activation (C42) is reasonable given the auto-activation mechanism and is validated by the observed downstream effects (JNK activation, apoptosis).

result: Prior literature establishes context for DLK and LZK function. DLK and LZK show context-dependent effects (pro-regenerative, pro-apoptotic, or pro-degenerative) depending on cell type and insult. They are associated with neurological diseases (PD, ALS, AD), show varied effects in different injury models, and are targets for drug discovery. Both kinases are expressed in cerebellum, with constitutive DLK knockout mice dying perinatally but adult deletion showing no abnormalities.
evaluation: Claims C4, C12-C45, C53, C61, C75, C81, C86, C94, C106, C137, C146-C147, C152-C153, C166, C168-C169, C178-C179, C186-C188 summarize prior literature establishing the biological context. These are appropriately cited and consistent with the field's understanding. They provide essential background but are not novel findings of this study.

result: Discussion and interpretation of findings. The authors conclude that controlling DLK and LZK activity is critical for neuronal survival, that DLK triggers strong/rapid responses while LZK induces modest/slow responses, that CELF2 regulates LZK but not DLK signaling through MKK7 splicing, and that the kinases act independently. They discuss implications for understanding neuronal stress responses and note that uncharacterized C-terminal domains may regulate signaling strength.
evaluation: Claims C11, C60, C87, C99, C114, C116, C149-C150, C162, C166, C170-C177, C180-C185, C189-C197 represent interpretations and conclusions drawn from the experimental data. These are generally well-supported by the results, though some involve speculation (C172, C176-C177, C190, C192, C194) which the authors appropriately qualify. The conclusions about differential signaling kinetics and CELF2/MKK7 pathway specificity are well-supported. Speculations about functional implications and future directions are reasonable but require additional validation.

result: Methodological details and validation. PvalbCre is active in Purkinje cells by P4. Molecular layer thickness is a sensitive measure of Purkinje cell dendrite disruption. The transgenic constructs include tdTomato reporters for expression monitoring. MAP2 is expressed in Purkinje cell dendrites. NF-200 is present in dendrites and axons and implicated in axon growth/regeneration.
evaluation: Claims C54, C52, C63-C64, C96-C97 provide methodological details and validation. These are supported by citations to prior literature and are consistent with standard practices in the field. They establish the validity of the experimental approaches used.

result: PvalbCre/+;Hipp11-DLK(iOE)/+ pups showed body weight loss, motor deficits, and early mortality. The authors note that PvalbCre is expressed widely in the nervous system, and since Purkinje cells are not essential for viability, the gross abnormalities and lethality are unlikely due to Purkinje cell death alone.
evaluation: Claim C167 and related discussion (C168-C170) appropriately acknowledge that the severe phenotype likely involves multiple cell types beyond Purkinje cells. This is a reasonable interpretation given the widespread expression of PvalbCre and the severity of the phenotype. The authors appropriately note this limitation and do not overinterpret the Purkinje cell-specific effects.
